In Java collections and object-oriented design, sorting elements relies heavily on two foundational interfaces: java.lang.Comparable and java.util.Comparator. When dealing with the question of which one modifies the original class, the answer is definitively Comparable. Comparable represents a natural ordering for a class, meaning the class itself must implement the interface and override the compareTo(T o) method, directly modifying its source code to dictate how its instances compare against one another. Examples of this include String, Long, and Integer, which are inherently sortable.

Conversely, Comparator is an external strategy pattern implementation. It decouples the sorting algorithm from the data model entirely. By creating a separate class or lambda expression implementing int compare(T o1, T o2), you can define multiple arbitrary sorting sequences (e.g., sorting employees by salary, name, or tenure) without touching a single line of the original Employee domain class. This makes Comparator exceptionally powerful when you do not own the source code of the class or when you require dynamic, runtime-defined sorting strategies.

rows: No (implemented externally as a separate strategy)
Multiple (as many custom strategies as needed)

items: The Comparable interface relies on the class's internal state. Its contract dictates that if x.compareTo(y) < 0, then y.compareTo(x) > 0, and transitivity must be strictly maintained to prevent undefined behavior in sorting algorithms like TimSort.

Comparator leverages modern Java functional programming features, allowing static helper methods like Comparator.comparing(), thenComparing(), and reversed() to build complex, multi-field sort criteria fluently.

When a TreeSet or TreeMap uses a custom sorting mechanism rather than natural ordering, it strictly requires a Comparator passed to its constructor; otherwise, it casts the inserted elements to Comparable at runtime, risking a ClassCastException.

parsed_answer.content: A classic production bug surfaces when a custom Comparator's compare logic is inconsistent with equals(). If your Comparator returns 0 for two distinct objects that are not considered equal by equals(), putting them into a sorted set like TreeSet will cause the set to silently drop elements because TreeSet relies on compareTo/compare rather than equals() for uniqueness checks.

title: Explain Comparable vs Comparator interfaces. Which one modifies the original class?
